title: Edda and the Paperwork Bridge
markdown:
High among the Whispering Peaks, where the air bit like a frost-apple and dawn used rose and gold without asking permission, lived Edda. She was as sturdy as an oak that had decided to remain. Her eyes were moss after rain. Her hands, large enough to shift a young pine, were better known for terraces of pumpkin and mountain phlox, and for the polished stones she lined on the windowsill, each one a kept night.

Biscuit went with her. He was a mastiff the colour of good earth, a bark like weather over the next ridge, a tail that argued for gentleness. Edda had found him a shivering pup by a ruined watchtower where mist slept among skeletal firs. She had scooped him up and talked the chill out of his bones. After that they shared a language of glances and floor-thumps. He was an anchor with paws.

One bright morning she packed a satchel and hummed. Elder Maeve, her grandmother, lived by a crystal lake in a higher pass and needed Moonpetal, which bloomed one week a year on the north face of Mount Cinder and was said to soothe old bones and make sleep kinder. “A useful errand,” Edda told Biscuit, scratching the velvet of his ear. He woofed in the affirmative and put a wet nose into her palm.

They took the old path. Narrow passes made their boots sound official. Sheer rock threw the sound back. Tiny blue gentians and proud yellow alpine buttercups held their colour against air that had less of itself than valleys do. A hawk hung on a nothing of wind. Biscuit’s paws made soft thuds on moss where the trail allowed moss, and clicked where it did not. Edda hummed the same tune she packed with, a cheerful thing that belonged in a kitchen and somehow worked on stone.

The way, worn by people who had needed grandmothers before, brought them at last to a deep chasm — a pause in the mountain’s sentence — spanned by a stone bridge that looked proud of its arches and entitled to an audience. On a stool at the entrance sat a person no taller than Edda’s knee, uniform stiff enough to stand without her, badge gleaming as if it had opinions about travellers. A ledger overflowed. A quill waited. This was Bronwen, the Bridge Keeper.

“Halt,” Bronwen squeaked, louder than her size. “No one crosses the Chasm of Contemplation without proper authorization.”

Edda’s brow made a small fold. “Authorization? I am visiting my grandmother. I intend a cup of chamomile and, if the bridge likes compliments, a look at the masonry. Not contemplation as a hobby.”

Bronwen adjusted spectacles that were conducting a precarious career on her nose. “Precisely. Intentions must be declared. Form 7B, Declaration of Inter-Passage Purpose. Form 12C, Pre-Passage Personal Potability Proclamation — confirming adequate drink before travel. Bridge Regulations, subsection Gamma, paragraph four.”

Edda’s eyebrows considered her hairline. “New?” Biscuit offered a growl that meant confusion.

“Ah, but here is the thing.” Bronwen tapped an overflowing ledger with a quill too large for the hand that held it. “New. Official. Vital for order and for the structural strength of paper. Without them, forbidden.” She pointed at a tower of parchment leaning on a boulder, a stack she could not have shifted if the chasm depended on it. “Triplicate. Black ink, approved shade, no smudges. Each signature witnessed — which I can provide. A small reasonable fee.”

Edda, who had walked through rockfall and blizzard without making a fuss, felt a bewilderment that had nothing to do with weather. She looked at Biscuit. His head tilt asked if this was a joke. She took mountain air into her lungs and tried logic, which the stool did not appear to stock.

“I drink from the Glacial Stream,” she said, a rumble that promised rain rather than storm. “My grandmother is unwell and waiting for Moonpetal. The view from this spot is already quite enough contemplating. Could I offer a direct account of my intentions instead of the forms?”

Bronwen puffed her small chest. “Regulations. An important bridge. Ministers of Mountain Affairs never travel without completed paperwork. Never.”

“What makes it so important that it needs hydration in triplicate?”

“It is… sturdy. A marvel. Important bridges require paperwork to prove they are important and sturdy. A preventative measure. Professionalism. The paperwork must flow.”

Edda saw it then: not malice, but a person clinging to rules the way a swimmer clings to a board. Importance, homemade, in ink.

She stepped close enough that her shadow fell softly. “You have a serious job. Travellers accounted for. The forms are how you show the work — to us, and to yourself.” From the satchel she took a grey stone she had polished until it held the sky. “The bridge is magnificent. I, Edda, of people who respect earth and crossing, promise it is sturdy, important, and safe, and that I am hydrated. I will sign that promise with my thumb. If you, Bronwen, Bridge Keeper of the Chasm of Contemplation, will witness it here.”

Bronwen stared at the stone, then at Edda’s face, then at Biscuit, who supplied a quiet tail-thump. She had not been asked to witness a thumb on stone. It felt more solid than the unread stack.

She dipped the quill, then — with a flourish too elegant for the comedy of the stool — pressed her own small thumb beside Edda’s, a dark pebble on a larger one.

“There. Official. Sturdy. Important. Hydrated. You may pass.” The smile was real and slightly surprised at itself.

“Thank you.” Edda put the double-marked stone back in the satchel. They walked the proud arches. Far below, the chasm kept its thoughts. Biscuit licked her hand once, as if to file the incident.

The air cooled as they climbed Cinder. Pines conducted the wind into rumours. Biscuit read the path the way some people read ledgers: wild thyme, the memory of a hawk, a change in the dirt that meant water not far. The north face asked for careful feet and did not apologise for the asking. Edda placed her hands where the mountain allowed hands. Once, scree shifted; Biscuit’s shoulder was there, warm earth, and the shift became only a story they did not tell.

In a hollow of thin bright sunlight, sheltered as Maeve had described, they found the Moonpetal. Silver blooms like change the night had forgotten to pick up, a faint scent, a glow you could miss if you arrived with too much purpose. Edda gathered a few sprigs as if the plant might notice roughness, wrapping them in a cloth that had been waiting in the satchel for exactly this politeness.

Coming down, the sun left oranges and purples on the ridges, rose and gold bleeding into a blue that was already thinking about night. Mist gathered in the lower firs around the old watchtower, swirling until the stones looked briefly inhabited. Biscuit sniffed, decided the inhabitants were weather, and trotted on.

Maeve’s cottage windows were already lamps beside the lake, which had begun its evening work of holding sky. Edda put the Moonpetal in her grandmother’s hands. Maeve’s eyes, old and sharp, took in the herb, then the satchel’s extra weight. “You brought a stone as well.”

“A receipt,” Edda said. “The bridge required proof it was a bridge. We obliged it in mineral.”

Maeve turned the double thumbprint to the lamp, smiled in the language of laugh-lines, and put the kettle on. Chamomile, as promised, and a chair that knew Edda’s shape. Biscuit sighed against her knee, a rumble more satisfied than any form. The lake held the first stars. No one mentioned the way of the mountains. The tea tasted of having crossed, and of a grandmother who did not ask for triplicate.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
